title: Barbarossa Begins
subtitle: Surprise, resistance and the struggle to understand the opening day
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: The German assault disrupted the Soviet frontier deployment unevenly. Local resistance continued while headquarters struggled to establish the situation, restore contact and coordinate a response to simultaneous penetrations.
body:
A war announced after it had begun

At 12:15 p.m. on 22 June, Molotov began the broadcast announcing Germany’s attack to the Soviet public. The American ambassador, Laurence Steinhardt, reported it to Washington in a telegram sent at one. By then soldiers and inhabitants of the western regions had already endured hours of invasion. Molotov presented Germany as the violator of the nonaggression pact and summoned the population to resistance; his announcement supplied a national account of events that people along the frontier were experiencing locally and unevenly. The gap between the first attacks and the public broadcast did not mean that nothing had been done in the interval. It meant that military orders, diplomatic explanations and public knowledge were developing on different clocks. [1]

In Berlin, Goebbels read Hitler’s proclamation at 5:30 a.m., German summer time, according to the American embassy. It announced military action and invoked Finnish and Romanian participation. The public justification concealed the preparations traced in Before the Storm. The German and Moscow reports identify their times separately; they should not be treated as a single synchronized clock.[2]a

The military result of the day was immense but specific. Germany seized the initiative along a vast front, damaged Soviet aviation, penetrated frontier defences and disrupted the command systems on which an organized response depended. It did not destroy all Soviet military power or remove every obstacle from its path. Indeed, the coexistence of rapid penetration and determined local resistance was one of the day’s most consequential features. A formation could be fighting hard while the operational structure around it was collapsing; another could withdraw from a threatened position only to find German troops already beyond its intended destination. [3]b

German headquarters entered the day with an operation to execute. Soviet headquarters had to discover the battle while trying to direct it. A report of tanks behind a division could mean a reconnaissance patrol, a temporary penetration or the leading elements of a force cutting its retreat. Each demanded a different response. When telephone lines failed and headquarters moved, the time needed to distinguish them increased. Surprise therefore continued to work after the bombardment: the German advance was changing the situation faster than some Soviet commanders could establish it.

The air offensive and the destruction of information

The Luftwaffe attacked Soviet airfields in the opening hours, seeking to destroy aircraft before they could intervene and to impair the bases from which surviving machines would operate. The blows were especially damaging in the western sectors, where forward deployments and incomplete dispersal exposed aircraft and supporting infrastructure. Runways and parked machines were only part of the target. Fuel, maintenance facilities, communications and the personnel who made sorties possible belonged to the same system. An aircraft that escaped destruction could still become unusable if it lost its base, supply arrangements or connection with the formations it was meant to support. [3]

Kipp reports a Soviet-acknowledged total of approximately 1,200 aircraft lost on the first day, including 758 in the Western Special Military District. The concentration in the central sector compounded the danger facing Pavlov’s armies. These are attributed reported losses, not an aircraft-by-aircraft register or a figure directly interchangeable with German combat claims.[4]

Air operations attacked movement and observation as well as equipment. Bombed junctions delayed reserves, while reconnaissance helped German commanders follow Soviet columns. For the defenders, the loss of aerial observation made it harder to establish the destination and strength of a penetration. Surviving troops consequently faced a double difficulty: moving towards a threatened sector and discovering whether the position they had been ordered to defend was still usable.

Soviet aircraft continued to fly. Even so, damaged airfields and the loss of aerial observation made the ground situation harder to establish. Telephone lines were cut, headquarters displaced and roads severed. The disruption resulted from the combined assault; air losses alone cannot explain the collapse of contact between an army and its divisions.[5]c

Counting losses

What “destroyed” can hide

A combat claim estimates what an attacker has destroyed. An inventory records holdings, while a serviceability return records machines ready to fly. First-day loss totals answer a different question again. Their apparent precision must be read against the incomplete information left after the airfields were attacked.[4]d

Lithuania and the race for crossings

In the north, Wilhelm von Leeb’s Army Group North attacked from East Prussia into Lithuania. Erich Hoepner’s 4th Panzer Group provided the principal mobile force, with Georg-Hans Reinhardt’s XLI Motorized Corps and Erich von Manstein’s LVI Motorized Corps operating on separate but related axes. Küchler’s 18th Army and Busch’s 16th Army followed and fought across a much broader frontage. Their opponent was Fyodor Kuznetsov’s Northwestern Front, formed from the Baltic Special Military District, with the 8th and 11th Armies forward and the 27th farther back. The German aim was to penetrate, disrupt those armies and gain the approaches to the Western Dvina before a coherent new defence could be established. [6] [3]

The geography encouraged rapid movement along particular corridors rather than a uniform sweep. Rivers and bridges repeatedly narrowed the choices available to both attacker and defender. A crossing secured before demolition could allow a leading force to preserve momentum, while a destroyed bridge could require reconnaissance, engineers and a detour. Roads concentrated vehicles, making traffic discipline and the ordering of columns important. The first German successes created opportunities because Soviet forces had to respond to penetrations whose eventual direction was still uncertain. They did not abolish the physical constraints of the terrain.

Hoth’s 3rd Panzer Group crossed southern Lithuania as part of Army Group Centre. Its advance towards Alytus and the Niemen crossings formed the northern arm of the intended encirclement in Belarus. Hoepner’s forces farther north belonged to Army Group North and were driving towards the Baltic crossings. Nearby columns could therefore have different commanders and operational purposes.[6]

For Kuznetsov’s command, the consequence was immediate pressure on both front-line divisions and the formations intended to strike back. The 3rd and 12th Mechanized Corps offered the means for a substantial counterattack, but they were not concentrated in one ready-made striking group. Their units had to move, establish contact and receive coherent tasks while the German advance and air attacks were changing the situation. The decisive tank battles around Raseiniai still lay ahead. On 22 June the important development was the creation of the conditions in which those counterattacks would be attempted: Soviet mobile reserves were being asked to restore a front already losing its shape. [4]e

Brest and the two different meanings of resistance

Farther south, Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group attacked across the Bug in the Brest sector, supported within Army Group Centre’s operation by Kluge’s 4th Army. Hoth’s northern movement and Guderian’s southern advance were designed to reach beyond the main Soviet concentration, while infantry armies pressed the front of the salient. The route through and around Brest mattered because it opened the southern approach toward the interior of Belarus. The fortress itself, however, became a battle whose duration and human experience did not match the speed of the mobile advance passing beyond it. [6] [7]

Elements of Soviet units caught in the fortress organized resistance after the opening bombardment. Fritz Schlieper’s German 45th Infantry Division conducted the assault, encountering groups of defenders who did not always share reliable communications or a single functioning command. Laila Akhmetova’s study follows men of the 131st Light Artillery Regiment through this disruption. Their experiences were not uniform: the unit’s prewar identity did not mean that all its personnel were together when the attack began, or that all those caught in Brest followed the same route through combat and captivity. The battle continued beyond the first day, even as the wider front moved east. [8] [9]

Akhmetova reproduces a later recollection by Mikhail Dimurin, a radio specialist recruited in Alma-Ata in 1939. He described being wounded when a shell struck the club building; Konstantin Ovsyannikov bandaged him, and Dimurin then lost consciousness. He remembered regaining awareness in a column of prisoners held by the Germans, supported by comrades on either side. The account comes through a postwar publication cited by Akhmetova, not a diary written during the bombardment. Its value lies in the particular sequence it preserves: wounds, assistance and capture could follow before a soldier understood the wider battle. Such experiences coexist with the fortress’s continued resistance. They also explain why a later collective story of endurance cannot describe the fate of every defender. [8]f

Akhmetova reproduces the postwar recollection of Mikhail Dimurin, a radio specialist recruited in Alma-Ata in 1939. Wounded when a shell hit the club building, he was bandaged by Konstantin Ovsyannikov and lost consciousness. He recalled waking in a German prisoner column, supported by comrades. The account reaches us through a later publication cited by Akhmetova. It preserves one man’s sequence of injury, assistance and capture while other defenders continued fighting.[3][10]

That danger was not fully visible from every headquarters on the first day. Reports arrived late or incompletely; commanders went forward to establish contact and became harder for their own staffs to reach. The German advance was exploiting a system in which damage to one connection could deprive several levels of command of reliable information. A unit might receive an order appropriate to the situation hours earlier and carry it out just as the enemy’s movement made it harmful. The resulting confusion was an operational condition with identifiable causes, not evidence that Soviet soldiers lacked the will to resist. [5]g

Western Ukraine offers a different battle

Army Group South’s opening was less immediately decisive than the developments in the centre. Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group advanced with Reichenau’s 6th Army on the northern part of Rundstedt’s front, while Stülpnagel’s 17th Army attacked farther south. Their opponent, Kirponos’s Southwestern Front, possessed substantial forces and a command organization that retained more ability to respond than the rapidly dislocated headquarters farther north. Soviet resistance did not stop the invasion at the border, but it complicated the conversion of penetration into a large encirclement. The terrain and the distribution of forces would make the southern campaign follow its own pace. [5]

The Soviet 5th Army under Mikhail Potapov covered the northern approaches in this sector; Ivan Muzychenko’s 6th Army operated farther south, with Fyodor Kostenko’s 26th and Pavel Ponedelin’s 12th extending the front toward the Carpathians. Kleist’s penetration threatened the relationship between the 5th and 6th Armies and opened the routes toward Lutsk, Dubno and Rivne, known in many contemporary accounts as Rovno. These towns mattered as road and railway connections as well as destinations. A counterattack against the flank of a German column in this area could threaten the route supplying it even if the Soviet force did not recapture every village already passed. [6] [11]

Delivering the southern counterstroke required a sequence of actions before any simultaneous attack could occur. Corps had to receive orders, travel to assembly areas, refuel, establish contact and bring supporting arms into position. Movement itself consumed the capacity being assembled: vehicles could break down, gasoline intended for combat could be expended on the road, and columns could become separated. A commander’s paper strength therefore differed from the force available at the moment an attack was demanded. These were mechanisms through which time and distance reduced usable combat power, and they help explain the uneven operations examined in the following chapters.

The contrast with Belarus was already consequential. Kirponos’s headquarters retained enough contact to organize resistance across several armies, even as its mobile formations struggled to assemble. That gave the Southwestern Front possibilities that Pavlov’s command was rapidly losing. It also left German commanders facing a penetration with substantial Soviet forces on its flanks. The southern battle would turn on whether those forces could exploit that position before German units cut their connections and routes of withdrawal. [5]h

Names on the map

Rovno, Rivne and the same road junction

Rovno in contemporary German and Soviet accounts is modern Rivne. Dvinsk and Dünaburg refer to Daugavpils; the Western Dvina is called the Daugava in Latvia. These equivalents help readers follow the same places across records written in different languages.[6]i

Moscow orders an offensive it cannot yet see

The central Soviet response developed through directives that became increasingly ambitious while the picture of the front remained incomplete. The second directive of 22 June ordered the destruction of enemy forces that had crossed the frontier and authorized air attacks into German territory. By evening, a third directive called for major counterstrokes. The Northwestern and Western Fronts were to converge toward Suwałki, while the Southwestern Front was to strike toward Lublin. The government was attempting to recover the initiative by imposing the offensive response anticipated in its planning on a situation already diverging sharply from that expectation. [3]

Counterattack offered a plausible means of exploiting the vulnerability of German flanks and supply routes. The difficulty concerned the relationship between that purpose and the condition of the forces ordered to execute it. The evening directives imposed distant objectives before headquarters had reliable knowledge of concentration, communications and enemy movement. An order might consequently direct troops westward while German formations threatened their routes to the east. Assessing the response requires comparing the desired operational effect with the information and capabilities available when the instruction was issued. Offensive intent alone establishes neither incompetence nor feasibility; the decisive evidence lies in how the task was connected to its means.

Zhukov reached the Southwestern Front on the first day as a representative of the high command. His later account, considered by Ziemke and Bauer, emphasized establishing the situation before launching a concerted operation. Commanders trying to determine what their formations could do were already under orders to advance. Their assessments struggled to reach the decisions quickly enough.[5]

The orders issued that evening left Soviet formations with little time to recover. Headquarters needed reports on losses and locations; commanders in the field needed fuel, ammunition and contact with neighbouring units. Yet the next task was already an offensive beyond the frontier. German commanders could exploit the interval between the decision in Moscow and the assembly of the forces meant to carry it out. Local resistance was continuing, but turning it into a coordinated counterstroke would be the central struggle of the next several days.

The evening directive made the distance between intention and capability measurable. It required the northern counterstroke to take the Suwałki area by the end of 24 June and the Southwestern Front to reach the Lublin area on the same timetable. Those objectives lay beyond the frontier, while Soviet headquarters were still struggling to locate forces and establish what had been lost. The demand to attack was therefore more than a general insistence on resistance. It bound an ambitious territorial result to a short interval in which formations first had to assemble, receive supplies and restore contact. The next several days would expose how far those necessary preparations lagged behind the orders. [3][18]j

The first day for civilians and prisoners

The Western Front’s report sent at seven on the morning of 22 June records how quickly the attack reached transport beyond the frontier positions. It reported two bombs dropped on a passenger train between Lida and Gavya, followed by machine-gun fire: ten people were reported wounded and the train was burning. It also recorded an attack near Bastuny. These are contemporary headquarters reports, not a later casualty census. They give a specific human and logistical consequence of the air offensive: a railway used to move people was already an exposed route, before commanders or travellers could possess a reliable picture of the invasion. The report does not identify the status of every passenger. [10]k

The populations affected did not share one relationship to Soviet rule. Some had experienced occupation, deportation, confiscation or imprisonment; others identified with the Soviet state or worked within its institutions. Jewish communities had particular reasons to fear German occupation, although knowledge of Nazi persecution did not always translate into knowledge of the killing policies about to unfold locally. No single photograph of a welcoming crowd, fleeing family or resisting soldier can stand in for all these experiences. The historian’s task is to distinguish them without treating hatred of one dictatorship as evidence of what the other would actually provide.

Prisoners were already entering a system prepared to deny them protection. The Commissar Order directed the murder of captured military political commissars; the May jurisdiction decree had weakened restraints on violence against civilians. These preparations were implemented from the invasion’s opening. Felix Römer’s research in German military records establishes that Wehrmacht units began executing captured political officers on the first day, across different sectors of the front. This finding goes beyond inference from the order’s existence: it documents military participation in the killings. It does not supply a verified total for 22 June or identify the fate of every captive. Capture, for the men selected under this policy, could lead directly from the battlefield to execution. [12] [13] [14]l

Soviet withdrawal also endangered people held in prisons. Security personnel preparing to leave threatened cities would murder prisoners in their custody. In Lwów, those crimes were followed by the persecution of Jews forced to handle the bodies. German and local antisemites exploited the killings to attack people who bore no responsibility for them. The 1 July study follows that sequence and distinguishes the perpetrators of each crime.

What the first day settled—and what it did not

Churchill’s broadcast on 22 June offered assistance to the Soviet Union while maintaining his condemnation of communism. Defeating Hitler now took priority over that hostility. The offer opened a new strategic relationship; the Soviet formations fighting that evening still depended on the resources already available to them.[15]

Washington’s statement followed on 23 June. Acting Secretary of State Sumner Welles condemned both dictatorships while identifying resistance to Hitler as serving American security. The invasion opened possibilities for cooperation whose practical requirements—Soviet requests, production, funds and shipping—still had to be settled.[16]m

Two announcements in one morning

Diplomatic notification after fighting began

Steinhardt’s report records Molotov saying that German ambassador Schulenburg notified him of the attack at 5:30 that morning, after military operations had begun. The public broadcast followed at 12:15. These times belong to the report of the Soviet announcement and should not be merged with the German proclamation’s separately identified summer time. The sequence shows why notification, public explanation and the beginning of combat require distinct entries in the chronology.n

[1]

The first day gave Germany a powerful opening towards its immediate objective: disrupting the frontier armies and obstructing their organized withdrawal. It created opportunities for encirclement. It did not establish that the Soviet Union’s reserves, industry or capacity to raise new armies had been destroyed. The distinction between those two results would govern the fighting that followed.[17]o

By evening, German operations had placed whole Soviet armies in danger by combining penetration with disruption of the systems needed to direct a response. Soviet resistance survived in many places, but its local effectiveness could not compensate for the loss of connections between formations. The surviving formations now needed to recover contact with their neighbours and headquarters quickly enough to mount a coordinated response. The counterattacks around Raseiniai and in western Ukraine would test whether surviving troops and equipment could be brought together in time to interrupt the advance, rather than committed through a succession of isolated encounters.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the passages used. Soviet documents are accessed in published transcriptions, not as original archive files; their archival references are those printed by the editors. Orders establish intended actions, while reports preserve contemporary estimates and gaps. German operational histories are read with their dependence on German records and postwar testimony in mind. Perpetrator documents are distinguished from neutral counts, and later recollections from contemporary testimony. Lettered evidence notes retain detailed references and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the source register below.
